name: Machinist
description: Machinists cut metal to a tolerance — setting up lathes, mills, grinders and CNC machines, and deciding how a part on a drawing actually gets made. ⚠ The occupation is flat but replaces about 29,500 people a year, and the money is in setup and programming rather than in running the machine. ⚠ This page also covers the CNC machine operator role, which is the rung below and the one occupation here with a projected decline.
credentialNote: ⚠ No licence governs machining, and the credential that matters is NIMS — the National Institute for Metalworking Skills — whose certifications are awarded skill by skill rather than course by course, which is why shops trust them. Ask a programme which NIMS credentials its students earn. ⚠⚠ The other thing to ask about is INSPECTION: aerospace and medical work carries documentation and quality-system requirements that ordinary job-shop work does not, and those are the sectors in Florida that pay best.
bodyHtml:
What the work actually is

O*NET: machinists set up and operate a variety of machine tools to produce precision parts and instruments out of metal, including fabricating, modifying or repairing mechanical instruments and machine tools. The tasks name the craft — calculate dimensions using micrometers or vernier calipers; machine parts to specifications on lathes, milling machines, shapers or grinders; measure and test completed units for defects and conformance to specifications; set up, adjust or operate specialized machine tools; program computerized or numerically controlled machine tools.

⚠ Measurement is the job as much as cutting is. A machinist who cannot measure reliably produces scrap confidently, and the inspection habit — check, record, check again — is what separates the trade from machine operation.

Projected need — and the honest version of it

O*NET, on federal projections: 299,500 machinists employed (2024), growth “little or no change”, 29,500 openings a year, median wages $58,750 (2025). For CNC tool operators the picture is similar and slightly lower: 177,100 employed, a projected decline of 1% or lower, 13,500 openings a year, median $50,690.

⚠ Neither occupation is growing, and both replace people steadily. Around 43,000 openings a year between them, in a trade with an ageing workforce — so the jobs are real while the headcount is flat. ⚠⚠ What that means for a student is specific: do not enter this trade to be an operator. Machine operation is the part most exposed to automation and the lowest paid; setup, programming and inspection are where the work holds.

⚠⚠ Operator, setup, machinist — the ladder is the point of the programme

Florida's 1,500-hour framework is deliberately a ladder with four hireable exits, and the distinction between them is the career:

  • Machinist Helper (300 hours) — shop safety, measurement, hand skills, material handling.
  • Machinist Operator (300 hours) — running machines that someone else has set up. ⚠ This is the rung the CNC-operator occupation sits on, and the one to pass through rather than settle on.
  • Machinist Setup Operator (600 hours) — work-holding, tooling, offsets and first-article inspection. The first genuinely skilled rung.
  • Machinist (300 hours) — reading a drawing and deciding how the part gets made: process, sequence, fixturing and tolerance.

⚠ Every rung above the operator is a judgement job, and judgement is what the automation has not taken. A shop can buy a machine; it cannot buy someone who knows why the part is out of round.

⚠⚠⚠ A small footprint for a fundamental trade

Eighteen Florida public institutions award a machining credential of some kind — machine shop technology, machine tool technology or CNC machining — but the state framework's own courses are carried by only five to seven: Atlantic Technical College, Immokalee, Manatee, Orange Technical College South, Palm Beach State, Pinellas Technical College and Suncoast. ⚠ The gap is colleges teaching the subject under their own college-credit numbers rather than the clock-hour framework. Compare welding, in the same CIP series: 47 institutions.

⚠ So this is a relocation or commute decision for much of the state, and it is worth knowing before you plan on it. Where no programme is nearby, the realistic routes are an apprenticeship with a machine shop, the college CNC certificate added to existing shop experience, or the welding and manufacturing programmes that are far more widely available.

⚠⚠ CNC machine operator — the same shop, a different job

“CNC operator” and “machinist” are used loosely in job adverts and they are not the same occupation. The federal data separates them, and the gap is worth seeing before you choose a programme:

CNC tool operatorMachinist
Employed (2024)177,100299,500
Projection to 2034⚠ decline of 1% or lowerlittle or no change
Openings a year13,50029,500
Median wage (2025)$50,690$58,750
Usual entry48% high school diploma33% post-secondary certificate

O*NET describes the operator's day as setting up and operating computer-controlled machines or robots to perform one or more machine functions; mounting, installing, aligning and securing tools, attachments, fixtures and workpieces; measuring dimensions of finished workpieces to ensure conformance to specifications; stopping machines to remove finished workpieces or to change tooling.

⚠ That is real, skilled work and it is a legitimate first job — the Machinist Operator course above is exactly this rung, and plenty of people start there. What the numbers say is that it is a rung, not a career: it is the one occupation on this site with a projected DECLINE, it pays about $8,000 less at the median, and it is the part of the trade most exposed to automation, because running a proven program is what a machine can be left to do.

⚠ The move up is setup and programming. Deciding how the part is held, which tools cut it, what the offsets are and whether the first article passes — that judgement is what keeps paying. If you take an operator job first, ask on day one what it takes to be trained on setup, and treat that as the objective.

Necessary skills

  • Measurement, obsessively. Micrometers, calipers, indicators, gauge blocks — and knowing the difference between a measurement and a reading.
  • Blueprint reading and GD&T. ⚠ Geometric dimensioning and tolerancing is the language a drawing actually speaks, and it is where beginners lose parts.
  • Mathematics you use every hour — trigonometry for angles and hole patterns, speeds and feeds, offsets.
  • CNC programming and editing. G-code, conversational control, CAM output — and the ability to read a program rather than only to run it.
  • Patience with setup. Most of the time is spent preparing, not cutting; the people who rush setup make scrap.

Advice

  • ⚠ Aim past the operator rung from the start. The pay, and the protection from automation, are in setup, programming and inspection.
  • Get NIMS certifications if the programme offers them — they are the credential shops recognise, and they are awarded per skill rather than per course.
  • Learn to inspect. Quality inspection is the adjacent occupation, it pays comparably, and it is far less physically demanding late in a career.
  • Florida's work is specific: aerospace and space-launch suppliers, medical devices, marine, and the job shops that serve them. ⚠ Aerospace and medical work means tighter tolerances, real documentation and better pay — ask a programme whether its graduates go there.
  • If no programme is near you, ask local machine shops about apprenticeship directly. This trade still trains people that way, and a helper certificate plus a willing shop is a legitimate route.
